content: Ensuring equitable access to PrEP can lead to improved health outcomes for individuals at substantial risk of HIV and their sexual partners. Many individuals at high risk of HIV are underserved, face barriers to accessing healthcare, and have limited prevention options. PrEP provides an opportunity to engage these populations in healthcare, including sexual and reproductive health services. Expanding PrEP recommendations beyond narrowly defined groups, such as men who have sex with men or serodiscordant couples, promotes equitable access and reduces stigma associated with targeting specific risk groups. Effective PrEP services can also lower future treatment costs by preventing new HIV infections in high-incidence populations. PrEP has been shown to be acceptable across diverse populations, including cisgender women (including pregnant and breastfeeding women), serodiscordant couples, female sex workers, young women, people who inject drugs, transgender individuals, and men who have sex with men. A review of 131 peer-reviewed articles and 46 abstracts revealed significant interest in PrEP as an additional HIV prevention option. Population support for PrEP is often based on its safety, effectiveness, and compatibility with other prevention strategies. Providing oral PrEP to diverse populations has been demonstrated as feasible in various trial settings, demonstration projects, and national programs. While placebo-controlled trials among cisgender women identified barriers to uptake and adherence, open-label PrEP studies have shown high adherence rates among women. Projects such as the iPrEx OLE and the Partners Demonstration Project confirm the feasibility of PrEP implementation for men and women. The PROUD study in the United Kingdom demonstrated that PrEP is both feasible and effective without significant changes in behavioral risk. Other demonstration projects in Botswana, South Africa, Thailand, and the United States have shown that most PrEP users can achieve protective levels of adherence, although challenges remain for some young people. By 2019, PrEP use was reported in 77 countries, and global usage continued to grow in 2020 despite disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Over 100 countries have adopted the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations on PrEP into their national guidelines. WHO published a comprehensive implementation tool for oral PrEP in 2017, which includes practical guidance for clinicians, laboratory monitoring, pharmacy services, testing, counseling, community engagement, and service integration. This tool is being revised for 2021–2022. PrEP should complement, not replace, other established HIV prevention interventions such as condom use and harm reduction strategies. Stigma, a significant driver of HIV, can either decrease or increase depending on how PrEP is implemented. PrEP should be promoted as a positive choice for suitable individuals and their communities, alongside other prevention interventions and services, including sexual and reproductive health services. Legal environments that violate the rights of people at substantial risk of HIV may pose barriers to PrEP implementation. Healthcare providers should be trained to discuss sexual and injection risk behaviors with clients, assess their HIV risk, and explore prevention options, including PrEP. Providers must offer respectful and inclusive services, understand trauma experienced by at-risk populations, and address barriers to healthcare engagement, adherence, and self-care. Services tailored to young people, especially young women and key populations, are essential for the success of HIV prevention programs, including PrEP. Providers should consider the health, social, and emotional needs of PrEP users and offer or refer them to appropriate services, such as mental health support, intimate partner violence services, family planning, and sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing and management. PrEP services can involve various healthcare and lay providers, including nurses, pharmacists, and peer providers, to reduce barriers to uptake and adherence. Community-based organizations, particularly those led by key populations, play a critical role in delivering PrEP services, engaging at-risk individuals, and linking them to other health and social support services. PrEP should always be provided as part of a combination prevention strategy, alongside interventions such as harm reduction and condom distribution. HIV testing is required before starting or restarting PrEP and should be conducted regularly during PrEP use, typically every three months. Additional testing after one month of PrEP use can detect acute infections that may have been present at initiation. Frequent HIV testing during PrEP use also provides opportunities for STI screening and management. Monitoring renal function is important for PrEP users, as reduced kidney function (creatinine clearance <60 mL/min) is a contraindication for tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)-based PrEP. Screening for creatinine clearance is recommended for individuals over 30 years old or those with comorbidities such as diabetes or hypertension. For younger individuals without kidney-related comorbidities, creatinine screening may be optional. Abnormal creatinine clearance should be confirmed before discontinuing PrEP, and other HIV prevention options should be discussed with the client. PrEP services also provide an opportunity to screen for hepatitis B and C infections. Testing for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) at PrEP initiation is preferred, and vaccination may be considered for those at risk. TDF-based PrEP is active against hepatitis B, and withdrawal of therapy can lead to relapse, although this is rare. Hepatitis C antibody testing can be considered at PrEP initiation and annually thereafter, depending on the local epidemiological context. Adherence support is crucial for PrEP effectiveness. Brief, client-centered counseling that links daily medication use to routine habits may improve adherence. Tailored interventions may be needed for specific groups, such as young people. Support groups, including social media groups, can facilitate peer-to-peer sharing of experiences and challenges. PrEP use is typically not lifelong and can be discontinued when a person is no longer at substantial risk of HIV. Engaging with PrEP users and community support groups can help identify periods of substantial risk and guide appropriate use. Event-driven PrEP is an effective strategy for cisgender men who have sex with men, involving a double dose of PrEP 2–24 hours before sex, followed by single doses 24 and 48 hours after the first dose. This approach is not suitable for other populations, such as cisgender women or transgender individuals engaging in vaginal sex, who require seven consecutive days of PrEP to achieve protective levels. WHO plans to release revised guidance on starting and stopping PrEP for all populations. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are associated with substantial HIV risk in some settings. TDF-based PrEP has been shown to be safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Antenatal and postnatal care services offer opportunities to integrate PrEP for women at substantial risk of HIV, but more research is needed to address the unique needs of this population. Operational research is needed to address challenges with PrEP uptake, effective use, and continuation, particularly among adolescents and young people. Innovative platforms, such as social media and mobile applications, can engage potential and existing PrEP users. The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated trends toward simplified and community-based PrEP delivery, including telehealth consultations and home delivery. However, more research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and scalability of these approaches. Research on PrEP should consider diverse biological, behavioral, and social outcomes, as well as how to integrate PrEP with other health and social services. High prevalence and incidence of STIs among PrEP users highlight the need to integrate STI screening and treatment into PrEP services. Similarly, integrating PrEP with reproductive health services could lead to broader health improvements. Family planning services may provide an opportunity to offer PrEP, but more evidence is needed on real-world program integration. More research is needed on the specific needs of transgender individuals, non-binary people, and people who use drugs, including how to improve awareness, uptake, and adherence to PrEP. People in prisons and other closed settings are often at substantial risk of HIV but are not adequately reached by prevention services, including PrEP. WHO has released guidance on event-driven PrEP for cisgender men who have sex with men, but global awareness and use of this approach remain low. Further work is needed to raise awareness and provide options for various PrEP dosing regimens.
